title: On Exchanging
subtitle: The Strategic Art of Liquidation
summary: Why exchanges should never be automatic: trading to tear open a file, eliminating vital defenders, avoiding tempo loss, and simplifying into a winning endgame.
aphorism: Never exchange simply because you can. An exchange is a surgical strike designed to seize a file, destroy a defender, or transition into victory.
attribution: 100th Anniversary Centenary Edition. Newly authored prose and interactive studies inspired by Aron Nimzowitsch (1925).

body.historicalContext: Amateurs often trade pieces when they don't know what else to do. Nimzowitsch treated the exchange as a decisive positional transaction that alters the landscape of the board.

sections.title: Exchanging to Open a Line
sections.markdown:
An **[[exchange]]** should always serve a concrete strategic aim. One of the most common reasons to trade is to **blast open a file** for our rooks.

By playing **cxd5**, White forces an exchange of pawns that clears the c-file for the white heavy pieces.

moves.comment: Black is forced to recapture, opening the c-file.
White immediately occupies the new open highway!

sections.title: Destroying the Key Defender
sections.markdown:
Another profound reason to exchange is to **eliminate a piece that guards a vital strategic square**.

If the opponent has a knight guarding the critical central outpost (e.g. e5 or d5), eliminating that knight clears the way for your own troops to conquer the outpost without opposition.

moves.comment: Pinning the knight defending d5 and e4.
White executes the exchange, removing the key central defender!
White prepares to seize the center.

drills.title: Liquidate for the File
drills.markdown: Trade pawns in the center to crack open the c-file for your rooks.

hints.text: Capture Black's pawn on d5 with your c-pawn.

feedback.correct: Spot on! The c-file is now an open highway for your rooks.
feedback.wrong: Capture on d5 (cxd5) to open the file.
